newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK fund-raising flurry seen persisting in 1996.
newsitem.headline: HK fund-raising flurry seen persisting in 1996.

text.p: A recent flurry of fund-raising activity on the Hong Kong stock market is expected to continue throughout the year as issuers capitalise on market buoyancy to raise a maximum amount of funds, analysts said on Monday.
"The market is high. They can get a better valuation (when raising funds)," said Alan Hutcheson, research manager at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

The Hang Seng was approaching within 100 points of its 1996 high in late August, before falling back to lower levels last week. On Monday, the blue chip index was down 47 points at 11,112.18 compared to a year high of 11,600.22 and a low of 10,070.79.

"When the market is at these levels, many people see share prices peaking. They think the market is fully valued and upside potential is limited," said Alex Tang, research director at Yamaichi International (H.K.).
He said the time was therefore ripe to raise funds.
Investors have been offered a wide array of share placements, warrant issues and initial public offerings (IPOs) in recent months.

In July and August, local firms made at least 12 share placements, three warrant issues and seven IPOs, including two spinoffs. Merchant banks launched at least 44 warrant issues, including many on blue chips and several on baskets of stocks.
Analysts said more than 20 companies were planning to list in Hong Kong before the end of the year.
Strong interim results of major companies, especially banks and property counters, have given market sentiment a boost.
China's recent interest rate cut and relaxation of its credit control were also contributing to a buoyant market tone by boosting the shares of China-related companies.

"That will create additional demand for quality H-shares and other Chinese companies, particularly if they can demonstrate that they have the management expertise and ability to benefit from an improving economic outlook in China," said Hutcheson.
Analysts said better business conditions in China were also encouraging companies to expand or embark on new projects there, prompting the need for more funds.
They noted China-backed companies and H shares -- China-incorporated enterprises listed in Hong Kong -- have been among the active participants in the recent fund-raising blitz.

"I expect a certain extent of fund-raising activity in the rest of the year," said Ben Kwong, research director at Dharmala Securities. "The market may be digesting previous fund-raising exercises now. They will be more active (later) in September."
Tang said the weak price performance of some recent listings should not deter new IPOs from coming to market as investor sentiment remained largely positive.
H-shares' fund-raising programmes would not flinch in the face of generally weak interim results as investors saw limited price downside and were ready to hunt for bargains, he said.
